title: The central limit theorem in plain language

videos.script: Here are Horta's four hundred baskets again. A peak on the left, a long tail to the right. Nothing like a bell. {{baskets}} Now draw five baskets at random, and write down their average. Do it again. And again. Two thousand times. {{five}} Draw a histogram of those two thousand averages. It is still lopsided, but less than the baskets were, and narrower. {{hist5}} Now do the same with samples of thirty. The histogram of the averages is almost symmetric. A bell. {{hist30}} With samples of a hundred, it is a narrow bell, centred exactly on the true mean of all four hundred baskets. {{hist100}} Nothing about the baskets changed. What changed is that you are looking at averages, and averages of random samples settle into a bell shape whatever the data underneath looks like. {{settle}} That fact is called the central limit theorem. It is the reason a sample of a few hundred can tell you about thousands, and every confidence interval and test in the rest of this course rests on it. {{rest}} This lesson shows it happening, says exactly what it promises, and says what it does not. {{promise}}
